title: The Mosque Built in a Dream

pages.text: On a school trip to northern Ghana, Mariama and Abdul-Rahman stopped in the village of Larabanga, near Mole National Park. A small whitewashed mosque stood before them, with two pyramid-shaped towers and strong buttresses along its walls. “It looks like a sandcastle that grew up,” said Abdul-Rahman.
sentences: On a school trip to northern Ghana, Mariama and Abdul-Rahman stopped in the village of Larabanga, near Mole National Park.
A small whitewashed mosque stood before them, with two pyramid-shaped towers and strong buttresses along its walls.
“It looks like a sandcastle that grew up,” said Abdul-Rahman.
pages.alt: Two students and a teacher look at a small whitewashed mud mosque with two towers.

pages.text: Mr Iddrisu explained. “It is built in the Sudanic style, of adobe, which is mud and clay, with wooden supports. It is about eight metres by eight metres, with twelve buttresses holding the walls. It is a place of worship, so we visit only as the community allows.” Alhaji Seidu greeted them with a smile.

pages.alt: An elder welcomes visitors outside the mud mosque.

pages.text: “Let me tell you how the people of Larabanga tell it,” said Alhaji Seidu. “A trader named Ayuba was travelling and rested near a mystic stone. He dreamed that he must build a mosque there. When he woke, the foundations were already laid. And so he built.” Mariama listened without writing. “Thank you for trusting us with the story,” she said.

pages.alt: A trader sleeps near a stone as a faint glow marks foundations on the ground.

pages.text: “When was this?” asked Abdul-Rahman. “People say about six hundred years ago, in the fifteenth century,” said Alhaji Seidu. Mr Iddrisu added, “One source gives the year 1421, but it ties the date to this tradition, not to a written record we could find. So a historian would ask: how could we check it?” Mariama wrote: written records, dating materials, other buildings.

pages.text: “There is another story,” said Alhaji Seidu softly. “Local people believe that a Quran was sent from heaven to the imam of that time, in answer to his prayers. This is a matter of faith for us.” Mr Iddrisu nodded. “We record what the community says, with respect, and we do not need to prove or disprove it.”

pages.text: “Now, a different mystery, a science one,” said Mr Iddrisu. “In the 1970s, people covered the mud walls with sand and cement to protect them. It seemed a good idea. But cement is not breathable like mud, and it trapped moisture inside the walls. Termites then ate the wooden supports, and part of the mosque collapsed.”

Termites then ate the wooden supports, and part of the mosque collapsed.”
pages.alt: A cross-section of a wall shows trapped moisture and termites in wooden beams.

pages.text: “Then, in September 2002, a severe storm destroyed the mihrab, the niche that shows the direction of prayer, and the minaret, the tower,” said Mr Iddrisu. “The World Monuments Fund helped, and the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board led a restoration with advice from experts in earth building. They replaced the timber and re-plastered the walls the traditional way, with mud.”

pages.alt: Workers re-plaster a mosque wall with mud while a storm-damaged tower is rebuilt.

pages.text: Before leaving, Mariama wrote three lists. Told: the dream and the Quran, as the community tells them. Not confirmed in our source: the exact date. Learned: that a well-meant repair can harm a building if we do not understand its materials. “Tradition and science can sit together,” said Abdul-Rahman. “If we ask carefully.” Alhaji Seidu smiled. The end.

activities.question: What is the Larabanga Mosque mostly built from?
options: Adobe, which is mud and clay, with wooden supports

activities.prompt: The mud walls were covered with cement. What do you think could happen to moisture in the walls?
options: It could get trapped and damage the building
It would make the wall stronger

activities.question: Why did part of the mosque collapse after the cement was added?
options: Trapped moisture and termites damaged the wooden supports

activities.definition: A building material made of mud and clay, often dried in the sun.

activities.prompt: Put the mosque’s story in order.
items: A trader dreams of building a mosque.
The mosque is built of mud and wood.
A cement coating traps moisture and the building is damaged.
The mosque is restored the traditional way.

activities.prompt: A well-meant repair did harm. When have you tried to help and learned that you needed to understand more first?

glossary.definition: A building material made of mud and clay.
Supports built against a wall to make it stronger.
A tall tower attached to a mosque.
